column4: The brawl spreads by ties: each of the cook, customers and waitress joins, steps in, shouts for the police or flees by his own temper and ties, a wild blow can draw a bystander in, and the place reads the deed worse.

Buses are scenery by his ruling of 23 Sep, so no lift happens on a bus; on the street the blueprint contradicts itself (1.6.13 has a lift with fixed limits and suspicion of people he noticed, CS-29 says pickpocketing is not a verb).

He can knock the man out and put him in a boot in 4 s, and anyone who sees it reads a killing seen at the grave band, but nothing says what the man does when he wakes in the boot (out lasts only 10 s to 5 minutes), and the Hook has the dock, not a canal.
column5: An unconscious or held man keeps his own clock wherever he is put: he wakes on time, and in a boot or room he bangs and shouts as a noise at its reach, remembers what he perceived, and acts by temper once free.

column11: violence: holding a man in a boot

column4: A man held by the collar with a knife shown is a threat at 0.8 through the talk rule, not a shield; hostage-taking is out for now as a decision within canon, so the gate guards weigh only their own nerve and the clerk tells what he saw.

column6: Holding a person as one state

column8: high: gossip that changes with deeds

column4: A post is lost by the rival when its man is frightened off, beaten or poached, so Frank can empty them one at a time, but holding a post needs a man standing there by routine, so alone he cannot keep three, and RT2-09 conflicts with the story's posts (C-337).
column5: A post belongs to whoever is seen holding it and is feared there: Frank holds one while present and his name holds others for days by menace, after which the rival sends more men (revenge by outfit) unless a crewman stands there.
column6: Turf held by presence and fear

column4: Provocation counts: if the other man struck first, witnesses read Frank's answer lower (times 0.7) as long as he stopped when it stopped, but a man starts trouble only with cause, so nothing says what would make a mugger pick Frank.
column5: Robbers pick marks by what they see (cash shown, a lone man at a quiet hour, a weak look), so baiting works by showing those things, and witnesses then read who struck first; a known face or Frank's menace puts them off.
column6: Robbers choose marks by what they see

column4: He can drag the man to a boot and leave him at the station door; anyone who sees the carrying reads it as a killing seen, and the man wakes and tells the police what he perceived before he was struck.
Only drag, carry, a boot or the quay edge are written; a body cannot be placed in a seat, though anyone who sees a body moved reads a killing.
column5: A body or an unconscious man can be set down wherever a man can be dragged (a seat, a bench, a doorway) as a pose; anyone close enough reads breathing against stillness by the body rule, and a fare who sees a dead man in the car is a witness to a killing.
column6: Bodies as objects in the world

column4: Stacking bodies is out (bodies are dragged, not furniture), and nothing says what cold does to a man left in a cold store.
column5: Places harm by one rule: cold, water and smoke add harm to a man who cannot leave over time (in a cold store an unconscious man reaches critical after some hours), found by the store's next routine.
column6: Places that harm by one body rule

column4: Set climbing places are in by his ruling but none are written, the working crane is ruled in but not designed (gap 4.2.2), and pursuers' choice to wait or give up is not set.
column5: Climbing places are map data with heights and times, the same for pursuers; men below decide by temper (wait, call the police, throw things, leave), and a man up a crane is seen by everyone in sight.
column6: Climbing at marked places by one rule

column4: Watchmen keep routines as schedules; casing a place learns its hours as windows in the Ledger, and a calm watcher only sees where he faces, so a gap can be timed.
There is no lockpicking: a lock is passed by a key, a back way left open or loud force that shows for a day; whether he can lock it again behind him is not written.
column5: Every door holds a state (locked, unlocked, forced) that its owner's routine notices as a trace; with a key Frank can relock it and leave no trace, a forced lock cannot be hidden, and lockpicking stays out.
column6: Doors, keys and locks as one system

column4: He can enter by key, back way or force and searching a drawer makes about 2 m of noise, but running water or a radio masking his noise is not modelled.
column5: A listener's own nearby noise (a running bath, a television, a radio) cuts what he hears by its loudness, so a search under running water carries less; when it stops he hears normally.
column6: Noises mask other noises by loudness

column4: A noise at its reach draws a watcher to look and the radio is a usable object, but a radio switched on is not listed as a noise source, and a radio that comes on in an empty room is not read as odd.
column5: Every prop that makes sound has a reach and an oddness: a radio switched on draws a guard by reach, and a sound nobody should make (a radio in an empty room) makes him alert rather than merely uneasy.
column6: Any noise is a lure by reach

column4: Damage by hand covers a window, windscreen, van light or sign; tyres are not listed and nothing says a damaged vehicle cannot drive.
column5: Every object has damage states that change what it can do (a flat tyre stops a van, a cut wire kills a phone), each heard at its reach and found by the owner's routine, read by him as a message.
column6: Damage to any object changes what it does

column4: Nothing is written for a note; a cover story is a claim weighed by fit, but only when spoken.
column5: A note or message is a claim delivered without Frank there: the reader weighs it by fit (handwriting, what it asks, the hour) and acts by routine and temper, and later can tell who might have sent it.
column6: Messages and lies as claims weighed by fit

column4: A tail runs on the watcher ladder with the target looking back every 20 to 40 s and at corners; losing sight is not failing, Frank picks him up at the next place on his routine.
Buses are scenery by his ruling of 23 Sep, so Frank cannot ride one; a tail lost picks the man up at the next place on his routine.
Overheard talk is heard only within earshot and phones are the office's, boxes and some homes'; no bug or extension listening is written.
column5: Frank hears whatever a man standing where he is could hear, so a phone extension in the same building carries the other end of a call to him, and a listening device stays out as beyond a 1990 street man's reach.
column6: Overhearing by where Frank can hear

column4: Nothing says a phone line can be cut; a witness then walks to a phone box.
column5: Damage to an object changes what it does: a cut line silences that phone, which is a trace found when someone tries it, so a witness inside must walk to a box (the walk timer).
column6: Damage to any object changes what it does

column4: Only set climbing places exist and none are written, so a drainpipe is not a way in; the woman's television does not mask his noise.
column5: Climbing places are map data (some drainpipes and yard walls among them), and a television masks sound by loudness, so a careful climb under its noise can go unheard while a window forced is heard.
column6: Climbing at marked places by one rule

column4: He can carry an unconscious man over the shoulder and a hidden man is found only by search or routine, but a skip is not a place yet (no skip until real, 2 Oct).
column5: Any container a man fits (a skip, a shed, a boot, a cupboard) is a hiding place for a body or an unconscious man, found by the routine that opens it; a man waking inside makes noise.
column6: Bodies as objects in the world

column4: A body goes into a boot in 4 s and a search with cause finds it; a car sitting lower is not modelled.
column5: A body in a boot is an object with weight: the car rides visibly lower to anyone close who knows cars (a constable at a stop), a give-away, not a meter.
column6: Bodies as objects in the world

column4: Nothing lets Frank set a man on a bench; a man found unconscious is acted on by temper.
column5: A man can be set down on a bench as a pose; passers-by take him for asleep unless close enough to see blood or no breathing by the body rule, and the first routine that stops to rouse him finds the truth.
column6: Bodies as objects in the world

column4: The cleaner whose routine opens the lock-up finds the body, holds only the aftermath and reports or tells, and the inquiry starts.
Still in the dark he is at most a shape, but a torch lights what its beam falls on, so if the beam lands on him he is seen; there is no breath-holding verb and none is needed.
Orders are a held key and a word; a lit cigarette is a light point seen far off, but no signal at distance is written.
column5: An order can be given by any sign the crewman can perceive (a wave, a whistle, a cigarette flicked), so it reaches him only if he sees or hears it, and anyone else who sees it may read it as a signal.
column6: Orders reach crew only through their senses

column4: 1.6.13 lets Frank lift a letter from a pocket by fixed limits, while CS-29 says pickpocketing is not a verb; a postman's bag is in neither, and this conflict has no C- id.
column5: One rule covers lifting and planting a small thing on or from a person or his bag: fixed limits of attention, light and crowd decide if it is felt, a missing letter is noticed at its routine (the delivery) and suspicion falls on people he noticed.
column6: One rule for lifting and planting small things

column4: Set climbing places are in but unwritten, and a roof is not one; slates as a noise surface are not in the table.
column5: Climbing places are map data; a slate roof is a loud surface by the noise rule, heard below and in the rooms under it, so neighbours wake by the sleeper rule.
column6: Climbing at marked places by one rule

column4: A scrap of food quiets a yard dog for a while, and no verb harms an animal.

column5: Hiding places are data, cars included: a back seat hides only from a man who does not look in, a constable returning to his car looks in, and a forced panda car is theft from the police, read grave.
column6: Hiding places and vehicles as one data set

column4: Hiding breaks sight and doors creak at their reach, but a wardrobe is not named as a hiding place.

column6: Hiding places and vehicles as one data set

column4: Any noise draws a watcher by reach, but car alarms are not in the props and a doorman's choice to leave his post is not set.
column5: A car alarm is a noise source with its reach (rare in 1990); a man on duty walks to look only if his duty and temper allow and comes back by routine, others in reach look too.
column6: Any noise is a lure by reach

column4: Light is a value and watchers keep routines, but no searchlight or moving dock light is designed.
column5: Moving lights and watchers run on readable cycles from the place data (a lamp, a torch round, a gate light), so a dash can be timed against them by the light rule.
column6: Watch routines readable as patterns

column4: Step noise follows surface and a bare stair creaks at twice dry flags; shoes off is not a state.
column5: Footwear is a noise factor: shoes off lowers step noise on stairs and floors, costs speed, and is itself odd to anyone who sees it.
column6: Footwear and surface set step noise

column4: Vans and lorries have no design and nothing lets Frank ride hidden in one.
column5: Vehicles that carry goods are hiding places on their route: Frank can climb in while unwatched, rides to wherever the route goes, and is found if the loader or driver looks in; getting out is seen by anyone in sight.
column6: Hiding places and vehicles as one data set

column4: A shop bell rings at its reach and draws people by temper, a wired alarm brings a constable in minutes, and running or hiding then follows the chase and search rules.
Planting is not written, and lifting itself is contradictory (1.6.13 has it, CS-29 says pickpocketing is not a verb).
column5: One rule covers lifting and planting by the same fixed limits; a planted thing is found when the man is searched or finds it himself, and he suspects people he noticed near him.
column6: One rule for lifting and planting small things

column5: Keys are objects in places: seeing where one is kept is a Ledger fact, taking it is a lift or a break-in, and its loss is noticed at the routine that needs it (opening time).
column6: Doors, keys and locks as one system

column4: Nothing lets Frank ride hidden in a van.
column5: Vehicles that carry goods are hiding places on their route; he arrives where the van goes and gets out unseen only if no one is in sight when its doors open.
column6: Hiding places and vehicles as one data set

Yes: the body rule applies with force half again on a man who did not see it; beating a man who yields or begs is shown and read worse (times 1.6).

Yes: a loud deed heard at the force reach, the damage stays until mended, and the owner reads it as a message by morning.
Running ends a fight, but a man seen running from every fight loses menace with those who see or hear of it.

Bruises last a day or two and a black eye three days, shown, but the colour stages are not written (listed as content).

Fights are about a dozen blows; wet cobbles slip 1 time in 20, grabs pull clothes, and a constable's shout or a bystander ends them.

CS-13 gives the choke a chance to fail each second (about 1 in 30) and success rates like 58% even crouched in the dark, while his ruling of 25 Nov says an unseen takedown in reach works, failing only on what the man could notice; the man remembers being struck and his last sight, not Frank's face if never seen.
column5: A takedown is decided by what the target can perceive: if he does not see or hear Frank before reach, the hold works; failure comes only from a sound, a light or a look the player could read, and any chance is kept to the violent end, fixed to the save.
column6: Readable rules decide takedowns, not rolls

column4: The finder acts by temper (helps, fetches help or the police, robs him or walks on), the found man is a story that travels, and he wakes with a grudge and his last sight.
Hiding in a boot is like a doorway: unseen, but a search of that car finds him.
A bare stair creaks at twice dry flags and a dropped thing makes noise at its own reach; sleepers hear at a third and wake to a loud sound, then act as owners.
A crewman with low nerve or high mouth chatters unless ordered quiet, and a lit cigarette is a light point seen far in the dark.
A cover story is a claim, believed when the slots fit (clothes, reason for the hour, the cab outside) and the listener does not know better; a bad fit makes him uneasy.
Anything graspable the props list marks can be swung or thrown, each a data row with its own force, reach and breaking; a wrench works like the wheel brace, and spraying a man is out.
Conscious, he climbs out at the nearest ladder within a minute and may come back for revenge by temper; out cold face down, he drowns in about two minutes unless pulled out.
Hands up is a yield answered by the other side's temper and purpose: a man defending himself leaves, a robber robs, a rival's men may take him to their boss, a grudge may land a few more.
The fire can kill the man inside by the body rule and is read grave, but its spread to the houses is a named gap with no model.
column5: Fire spreads by material and wind through the place data, so a lock-up fire reaches a terrace only where timber and nearness let it, seen and smelt at its reach, with the brigade arriving.
column6: Fire spreads by material and wind

column4: He comes round where he fell or where he is taken: a rival's men take him to their boss for a talk and a demand, robbers take the paper money and what is under the coat, never the Ledger or keys.

Burns and scalds as weapons are out as cruelty under canon's content rule.

Buses, the ferry and boats are scenery and Frank cannot climb on a moving car, so no fight happens on anything moving.
Hostage-taking as a shield is out for now as a decision within canon: a man held with a knife shown is a threat at 0.8, not a shield the police respect.

A beaten man may come back by grudge at a time routines cross, but nothing says an ordinary man can follow Frank or what he learns by it.

He answers by his own temper (fights, backs off, yields, runs or shouts for help), watchers read the deed, and it travels as talk.
A threat folds a man if his nerve and pride are under its weight (a word 0.5, a weapon shown 0.8, plus Frank's menace); a threat stops a report, never the talk.
